# The Demand Side: Policymaker Perspectives on Open Technology Research - Open Technology Research

## The Demand Side: Policymaker Perspectives on Open Technology Research

- [Finding #1: Evidence is already part of how decisions get made, but its use varies widely](https://opentechresearch.org/blog/the-demand-side-policymaker-perspectives-on-open-technology-research/#finding-1-evidence-is-already-part-of-how-decisions-get-made-but-its-use-varies-widely)
- [Finding #2: Economic impact and business case remain the central gaps](https://opentechresearch.org/blog/the-demand-side-policymaker-perspectives-on-open-technology-research/#finding-2-economic-impact-and-business-case-remain-the-central-gaps)
- [Finding #3: Research needs to reach People through different channels](https://opentechresearch.org/blog/the-demand-side-policymaker-perspectives-on-open-technology-research/#finding-3-research-needs-to-reach-people-through-different-channels)
- [Finding #4: The geography of evidence is deeply uneven](https://opentechresearch.org/blog/the-demand-side-policymaker-perspectives-on-open-technology-research/#finding-4-the-geography-of-evidence-is-deeply-uneven)
- [Finding #5: AI has changed the stakes of the evidence gap](https://opentechresearch.org/blog/the-demand-side-policymaker-perspectives-on-open-technology-research/#finding-5-ai-has-changed-the-stakes-of-the-evidence-gap)
- [Implications for OTR’s research agenda](https://opentechresearch.org/blog/the-demand-side-policymaker-perspectives-on-open-technology-research/#implications-for-otrs-research-agenda)

*By: Nicholas Gates (OpenForum Europe)*

As part of developing the [Open Technology Research](https://opentechresearch.org/) (OTR) shared research agenda, the initiative conducted a series of interviews with policymakers and public sector practitioners across multiple regions and institutional contexts. These ranged widely, from national digital transformation agencies in the Global South to digital ministries in Asia Pacific and Europe to sub-national legislative staff in the United States.

The interviews surfaced a remarkably consistent picture: not of a field that lacks research, but of one that remains underdeveloped in its scope and consistently fails to deliver it in forms that policymakers can use. Why is this important? Well, with big moments yesterday like the [release](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1187) of the European Commission’s “Tech Sovereignty Package”, and its accompanying Open Source Strategy, it’s more important than ever to build the connections between researchers, practitioners, and policymakers necessary to feed evidence into policy-making.

This article summarises the (early) key findings from our ongoing conversations with policymakers. Our findings focus on how policymakers actually engage with evidence on open technology, where the most consequential gaps lie, and what the research community would need to do differently to have genuine influence on public decisions.

## Finding #1: Evidence is already part of how decisions get made, but its use varies widely

One of the clearest findings from the interviews is that, counter to public opinion, policymakers do not ignore evidence. Across different institutional settings – from a digital services unit inside a national presidency to a multilateral development bank to a state legislature – the interviewees described research and best practice as a routine and often indispensable input to their work. Many had built dedicated internal research capacity, commissioned independent evaluations, or embedded researchers within their teams.

Whether this trickles up to the very top remains uneven, but the people doing the work consume research regularly, and the same is true for the ever-growing field of open technology. In this sense, the demand is real. Nevertheless, the evidence base these decision-makers actually have access to is, more often than not, inadequate for the questions they face. The gap is not primarily about awareness or interest, but is structural: open technology research is fragmented, hard to discover, and rarely translated into the decision-ready formats that procurement officials, legislative staff, and ministerial advisors require.

Policymakers (or the staff that support them) frequently described doing substantial research internally – compiling comparisons, assembling business cases, conducting feasibility assessments, etc – precisely because the external evidence they needed did not exist or was not accessible in a form they could use.

## Finding #2: Economic impact and business case remain the central gaps

The single most consistently cited research gap is the absence of credible, comparable, and decision-ready evidence on the economics of open technology adoption.

Policymakers across regions and institutional contexts repeatedly returned to variants of the same problem: they needed to make a case to colleagues, budget officers, ministers, or elected officials for an open approach rather than a proprietary one, and the evidence to support that case was either missing or too thin to be persuasive. Several interviewees noted that the case for open technology is made on ideological grounds, while the case against it is made on economic grounds. Closing that asymmetry requires evidence that meets the needs of procurement sceptics and budget holders on their own terms.

What interviewees also described needing is not abstract macroeconomic analysis of the aggregate contribution of open source to GDP, however useful that work may be. They needed evidence that was more applied and concrete; for example, the total cost of ownership over realistic timeframes, including the costs of switching, sustaining, governing, and supporting open deployments. Or, evidence on return on investment that was credible to procurement officers who had been told, sometimes correctly, that open source isn’t actually free. They needed documented examples of open technology delivering measurable improvements in service quality, cost, or resilience, and they needed those examples to come from contexts similar enough to their own to be transferable.

Multiple interviewees said they had some of this data, but that they were receiving it anecdotally or through direct government-to-government knowledge sharing. This data was often unavailable, and they had to use proxies, but when they reached out directly, they were often able to access some version of it, even if it was incomplete and not comprehensive in the picture it provided. Figuring out a way to systematise the collection of such peer-to-peer knowledge could be a useful step for researchers and practitioners.

## Finding #3: Research needs to reach People through different channels

When asked what makes research land in their context, policymakers were consistent in their answers, and their ideas often diverged significantly from the dominant modes of academic and think-tank publishing.

Legislative staff, in particular, were explicit that research finds its audience primarily through major generalist publications, not through preprints, academic journals, or policy-focused think-tank reports. If findings are not accessible to a general reader – for example, if they require a technical background to interpret, or if they are buried in a format that legislative offices don’t routinely encounter – they will simply not reach the people making decisions.

The implication is uncomfortable but clear: publication alone, even publication in respected outlets, is insufficient. Research needs explicit partnerships with journalists and editors who reach legislative audiences, or it needs other channels. This could include regular briefings, direct relationships between researchers and staffers, or participation in standing fora where legislators and their teams already gather to engage with evidence. It also means publishing research and ideas in many different formats simultaneously as a default, rather than a long report coming first and maybe being supported by other, more consumable formats, if successful.

For policymakers in agencies and development institutions, the picture was somewhat different but pointed in the same direction. What was most valued were working examples such as demonstrations, prototypes, and show-and-tells, outputs that made abstract claims about open technology concrete and visible. Several interviewees noted that the abstractness of open source – the fact that it is often invisible to end users and difficult to illustrate – is itself a political liability, and that research capable of making it tangible through more visual or interactive formats performs a function that no amount of rigorous analysis can replicate.

Practical artefacts such as checklists, model contract clauses, evaluation frameworks, and procurement templates were also mentioned as having disproportionate impact relative to their apparent significance, and the translation of academic research into such outputs is critical for systematic knowledge sharing and peer-to-peer exchange. This was especially relevant for those working in multistakeholder fora like development banks and international organisations. The reason such formats work is straightforward: they translate research findings into tools officials can use directly, without requiring them to master the underlying literature first.

## Finding #4: The geography of evidence is deeply uneven

A thread running through interviews with practitioners in the Global South was the frustration of operating in a research environment built on evidence from elsewhere. Business cases drawn from high-income country deployments, sustainability models derived from the open source ecosystems of Northern Europe and North America, and governance frameworks shaped by the legal and institutional contexts of wealthy democracies. These are the most readily available materials, and they do not always travel.

This is not merely a representational complaint. It has direct policy consequences. When practitioners in lower-income countries face the question of whether to adopt a particular open platform, the evidence they need concerns implementation in contexts with different infrastructure, labour markets, procurement rules, and vendor ecosystems. When governments in the Global South consider open technology as a response to dependency on proprietary systems, the sovereignty argument takes on a different structural form: dependency relationships run South to North, and adopting a digital public good (DPG) maintained by a foundation based in another country raises its own questions about reliance and control.

Practitioners in this position reported lacking access to the evidence needed to answer questions specific to their context. This was not because no one had studied analogous deployments, but because the research community had not prioritised it, and there was a lack of local capacity building as a precondition for sustainable adoption and deployment. Moving forward, more understanding will be needed of how to create the institutional and country-wide conditions to make local knowledge available and shareable. In this sense, Open Source Program Offices (OSPOs) might offer a promising model for localising and diffusing research capacity, as well as feeding it back into government, but more will need to be learned from pilots underway across the globe.

## Finding #5: AI has changed the stakes of the evidence gap

Across virtually all interviews, artificial intelligence (AI) emerged as an area of acute and growing demand for evidence, and one where the gap between what policymakers need to know and what the research base currently offers is especially wide.

For legislative staff, the most pressing questions concerned accountability and transparency: how to understand what is happening inside AI systems, how to attribute harmful outcomes to identifiable decisions about training or deployment, and what the difference between open and closed AI actually means in practice for auditability, oversight, and public trust. The opaqueness of AI systems was described as actively corrosive to the relationship between legislators and developers — a trust deficit that research capable of illuminating model behaviour and architecture could begin to address.

For government agencies making deployment decisions, the questions were more operational but no less urgent: what assurance practices are actually required to use open AI models safely in high-trust public services, how to evaluate competing AI procurement claims consistently, and what the real-world performance gap between open and closed models looks like on dimensions that matter for public sector use. These are questions the research community is beginning to engage with, but not yet at the pace or scale that policy demands require.

## Implications for OTR’s research agenda

What the interviews make plain is that the demand for open technology research among policymakers is real, motivated, and largely unmet, but that meeting it requires more than just producing more research on the important topics highlighted in our research agenda.

Many new questions and ideas were highlighted in our interviews, of course, but, really, what policymakers in this context seem to want is ways to produce it differently, with particular attention to format and accessibility, as well as the channels through which evidence reaches decision-makers. There also needs to be more explicit investment in research partnerships globally, as well as an expansion of geographic coverage to give evidence from the Global South the same weight and reach as evidence from the North. Finally, direct engagement between researchers and the practitioners whose questions should be shaping the agenda will be vital.

OTR is designed around exactly this challenge: not just building a research network, but (eventually) building the infrastructure – discovery tools, partnerships, accessible formats, etc – that connects research supply to genuine policy demand. We hope to announce more on how such findings will help shape these modalities in the months ahead.

*This article draws on consultations conducted as part of OTR’s global engagement process. For more on the initiative and to contribute to review our*[shared research agenda](https://opentechresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Open-Technology-Research-A-Shared-Research-Agenda.pdf)*, visit*[opentechresearch.org](http://opentechresearch.org)*.*
